problem.canonical_name: Governed Semantic Context Layer for Agents and Activation
problem.plain: agreeing on what basic terms like "customer" mean

format.label: A memo to a CMO
format.instruction: Write it as a short internal memo to a chief marketing officer. Plain language, no jargon they would have to look up. Around 120 words.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Memo — Agent context, how I'd start

I don't think we should build a company-wide dictionary first. Those projects die in committee. Instead:

Pick the twelve numbers that actually appear in your board deck. Write one executable definition of each in the warehouse, owned by a named person. Agents may not compute those numbers themselves — they call the definition or they say they don't know.

Attach permissions to the definition, not the tool. One policy, checked every call, logged.

Treat the agent plumbing as disposable. Assume it gets rewritten yearly; keep the value in the definitions.

What I expect to hit: the disagreements are political, not technical. And row-level control inside ad platforms isn't really possible — we'll send aggregates there and accept that.

Measure wrong-but-plausible answers weekly, or we're guessing.
answers.first_move: Get the twelve numbers from the last board deck and ask each owner to write down, in SQL, what they actually mean.
answers.hardest_part: Two teams defining "active customer" differently is usually a real difference in how they're measured and paid, so agreeing on one definition means someone loses an argument about their own performance.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
To: CMO
Subject: Start with governed decisions, not a universal dictionary

I would not begin by standardizing every marketing term. That becomes a governance program with no end. Pick one valuable, bounded action—such as suppressing active customers from acquisition campaigns—and define every required term as a versioned contract: owner, source, calculation, exclusions, freshness and permitted uses.

Enforce access when the agent requests data, using the person, purpose and action involved. Return the definition, version and permitted scope with every result. Keep the MCP connection thin so protocol changes do not disturb meaning or policy. Run agents in shadow mode first, compare their decisions with human-reviewed outcomes, and require approval for spend, messaging or export.

This will not solve shared semantics industry-wide. It should reveal whether narrow, portable contracts can remain correct across systems.
answers.first_move: Choose one activation decision where a wrong definition would cause measurable harm.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is assigning authority when teams legitimately disagree on meaning while preserving permissions across systems that enforce them differently.

answers.label: Gemini
answers.approach: To: Chief Marketing Officer. From: Marketing Technology. Subject: Marketing AI agents and data governance. The standard advice is to build a company-wide data dictionary and wait for tech vendors to standardize security. That will fail; our departments do not agree on basic definitions, and the underlying tech standards keep changing. Instead of trying to give an AI agent universal access to our systems, we should strictly limit it to one narrow workflow, such as re-engaging lapsed accounts. For that single job, we manually define the three metrics that matter and give the agent a locked, read-only data feed tailored only to that task. We will not get an all-knowing marketing assistant, but we will avoid costly hallucinations and data leaks.
answers.first_move: Pick one single marketing campaign and build a private, read-only data view that exposes only the exact fields that campaign requires.
answers.hardest_part: Different teams have conflicting incentives to define key numbers like revenue or lead quality differently, making shared definitions an organizational battle rather than a software problem.

format.label: Three moves
format.instruction: Give exactly three moves, in order. One sentence each, then one sentence on what makes that move hard. Nothing else.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Move 1 — Stop negotiating definitions in documents and make every contested term an executable, versioned artifact in the warehouse (a semantic-layer measure with an ID, owner, and effective date), where agents may only reference definition IDs and are forbidden from composing their own filters. What makes it hard: the disagreement doesn't disappear, it relocates to who owns the query, and ad platforms and CRMs will keep computing their own 'customer' server-side where you cannot override it — so the deliverable becomes continuous reconciliation and published drift between your definition and theirs, not consensus.
Move 2 — Stop expressing permissions as tool scopes and push them into the data path: every agent call carries a short-lived token binding the human principal, the purpose, and the consent basis, and all reads go through one policy-enforcing gateway that applies row and column policy at execution time rather than at connection time. What makes it hard: delegated identity barely exists in martech SaaS — most APIs offer an app-level key with no notion of 'acting on behalf of, for this purpose' — so you are forced to proxy those systems and inherit their coarse audit trails, and purpose limitation is a legal concept that no IAM model natively encodes.
Move 3 — Treat MCP as disposable plumbing: keep semantics and policy in your own contract layer, generate the MCP surface from it, and gate every release on a regression suite of gold questions with known-correct answers and known-correct refusals. What makes it hard: authoring evals for ambiguity is far harder than authoring them for accuracy, because the ground truth is the very thing under dispute, and a stateless-vs-stateful spec change leaks through any abstraction that assumed session continuity.
answers.first_move: Pick the five terms that actually cause arguments and turn each into one owned, versioned query in the warehouse.
answers.hardest_part: The ambiguity is organizational, not technical — different teams need 'customer' to mean different things, and a semantic layer forces a decision nobody has authority to make.

answers.approach:
Move 1: I would reject the universal-ontology-first approach and define a small, versioned set of executable semantic contracts for two or three high-risk activation journeys, including owners, lineage, freshness, tests, and explicit context-specific meanings.
What makes this hard is that disagreements over terms such as “customer” usually reflect legitimate differences in business purpose, incentives, and accountability rather than missing documentation.
Move 2: I would create an authorization envelope carrying delegated identity, purpose, consent, tenant, policy version, and row- and field-level constraints, with a central policy decision point and deny-by-default enforcement at every tool boundary.
What makes this hard is that warehouses, CRM systems, CDPs, and ad platforms have incompatible security primitives, so some entitlements cannot be translated faithfully or revoked consistently during chained calls.
Move 3: I would place a gateway between agents and tools that compiles approved semantic contracts and entitlements into short-lived capabilities and typed views, then test it with replayable tasks designed to expose plausible-but-wrong outputs while isolating MCP changes behind adapters.
What makes this hard is proving semantic correctness across multi-step actions when source data, definitions, permissions, protocols, and vendor behavior can all drift independently.
answers.first_move: I would start with one high-risk activation workflow and write down exactly what every term means.
answers.hardest_part: The hardest part is preserving both meaning and authorization across systems whose data models, security controls, and rate of change do not align.

answers.label: Gemini

Force every agent data retrieval through a code-governed metric engine that compiles queries into deterministic, permission-checked semantic models before any downstream API is called. What makes this hard is that major marketing platforms rely on proprietary, walled-garden definitions that actively resist standardization into a shared semantic model. 2. Attach short-lived, cryptographically signed policy tokens to every agent payload to carry cell-level entitlements and user identity across tool invocations. What makes this hard is that passing verifiable access policies across fragmented, third-party marketing tools requires a federated authorization standard that does not exist. 3. answers.first_move: Force all agent data retrieval through a single metric repository with strict access rules instead of letting agents query operational marketing tools directly.
answers.hardest_part: Different business units have fundamentally incompatible, politically entrenched definitions for the exact same metric that software cannot magically reconcile.

format.label: Pseudocode
format.instruction: Express the approach as short annotated pseudocode. The comments should carry the reasoning; the code should carry the structure. Around 15 lines.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
```
# 0. Contrarian premise: a single canonical ontology is not achievable and chasing it is why
#    this has failed for 20 years (MDM, CDP "golden record", dbt metrics layer). Don't unify meaning.
#    Make disagreement explicit, owned, and machine-readable. That IS the deliverable.

registry = GitBackedDefs()                      # one file per term, mandatory human owner, no anonymous defs
for term in ["active_customer","qualified_lead","revenue"]:
    for sys in [crm, cdp, warehouse, ads]:
        registry.add(term, sys, expr, owner, as_of)   # N coexisting defs, each locally correct
    registry.flag_conflicts(term)               # the conflict report is the exec artifact that forces a decision

# 1. Agent carries zero ambient authority. It borrows the asking human's.
ctx  = on_behalf_of(user_token)                 # agent-owned service creds are the leak vector; ban them
plan = agent.plan(question)
for ref in plan.terms:
    if registry.conflicted(ref) and not plan.pins(ref, version):
        return ask_human(ref, registry.options(ref))   # refusing to guess is the highest-value behavior here

# 2. Push enforcement DOWN. A policy engine I own will drift from the systems of record within a quarter.
rows = warehouse.run(compile(plan), as_user=ctx)       # native RLS + column masks do the denying
aud  = ads.push(rows) if ctx.may(EXPORT, rows.cols) else aggregate_only(rows, k=50)
# honest gap: ad/CDP APIs authenticate by tenant service key. Identity does not propagate. A proxy with
# k-anonymity floors is a downgrade, not a fix, and I'd say so out loud rather than claim coverage.

# 3. Don't try to prevent confident wrongness. Make it checkable after the fact.
return Answer(value, def_hash, lineage, fields_declined)  # hash pins which semantics produced the number

# 4. Transport churn: the MCP server is a thin adapter, ~200 lines, assumed disposable.
#    Meaning and entitlements live in the registry + warehouse, which survive spec revisions.
#    KPI is not "agent accuracy" — it's cross-system definition divergence trending down, and
#    clarification-rate falling as owners resolve conflicts. If divergence is flat, the project failed.
```
answers.first_move: Pick the three terms executives actually argue about and write down every existing definition of each, with the name of the person who owns it.
answers.hardest_part: The definitions differ because teams are compensated on different numbers, so the blocker is an organizational decision no schema or protocol can make for them.

format.label: A checklist
format.instruction: Give a checklist someone could actually run next quarter. Each item concrete enough to be marked done or not done. Six items at most.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Up front, where I'd break from the obvious answer: don't try to agree on what "customer" means. That project has failed in every org I've seen because the disagreement is real — finance's active customer and lifecycle's active customer differ for defensible reasons, and someone's number moves if you force a merge. The achievable goal is governed pluralism: every definition is named, namespaced, owned, versioned, and the agent is forbidden from picking one on your behalf. Second break: I would not start with semantics at all. I'd start with the enforcement point, because an ambiguous answer is recoverable and a leaked audience isn't. Third: treat MCP as a disposable adapter, not an architecture — if your July 2026 rewrite cost more than a week, the semantics were living in the wrong place.

1. Conflict inventory, not a glossary. Pull 90 days of actual asks (BI tickets, Slack #data-help, any agent logs you have) and rank terms by how often they're asked and how much money moves on the answer. Take the top 10–12. For each, go find every definition already running in prod — CRM formula field, CDP trait, dbt model, the ad platform's own conversion window — and write down how many there are and where they disagree numerically. Done when you can say "'active customer' has six definitions in prod and they differ by 23% on the same month." Expect the number to be worse than leadership believes; that's the artifact that buys you the quarter.

2. One mediation proxy, delegated identity, enforcement pushed down. Every agent call to data or activation goes through a single gateway. The agent runs as a delegated human principal, not a service account; row filters and column masks live in the warehouse/CDP policy engine, not in middleware you wrote. No agent holds ad platform credentials directly. Done when the same prompt run as a regional rep and as the CMO returns provably different row counts, and you can produce the per-call log showing which principal and which policy applied.

3. A transport-neutral metric contract repo. Definitions in git, compiled to a static artifact: namespaced name, owner, SQL/logic, grain, valid time window, allowed activation destinations, deprecation date. Pluralism is legal — finance.active_customer and lifecycle.active_customer both ship — but an unowned definition cannot be published. MCP server is generated from this artifact and should be small enough that next spec revision is a week of work. Done when you can delete and regenerate the MCP layer in a day without touching a definition.

4. Make abstention the default failure mode. This is the item most teams skip and it's the one that actually attacks "confidently wrong." The agent may only answer from the compiled contract; if a term maps to zero definitions or to more than one in the caller's context, it must refuse and ask which, not improvise SQL or guess. Kill the raw-query escape hatch for agents in the governed path. Done when a red-team set of ~30 deliberately ambiguous and out-of-scope questions produces 30 refusals or clarifications and zero fabrications.

5. An eval harness that measures the right failure. 100 real questions with human-adjudicated gold answers, run on every change to definitions, prompts, models, or the MCP layer. The headline metric is not accuracy — it's confidently-wrong rate (answered, no hedge, wrong) which you track separately from refusal rate. Ship gate: confidently-wrong under some number you commit to publicly. Done when the harness runs in CI and has blocked at least one release.

6. Provenance that survives activation. Every audience, suppression list, or conversion payload leaving for an ad platform carries the definition ID and version in its name and in a stored manifest. Weekly job reconciles platform-reported match/counts back to the originating definition. Done when you can take any live audience in Meta or Google and name, in under a minute, which versioned definition built it and who owns it. Expect this to be where it hurts: destinations mangle your semantics, match rates hide drift, and you'll find orphaned audiences from people who left.

What I expect to run into: the entitlement model will not actually follow the agent across tools, because the ad platforms have no concept of your row-level policy — the honest mitigation is to refuse to let agents write directly to systems that can't carry the policy, and to accept a slower human-in-the-loop path there. Also expect the semantic layer to become a political queue; the owner field is the whole game, and if you can't get named owners with authority, stop and solve that instead.
answers.first_move: Pull the last 90 days of real questions people asked about the top business terms and count how many conflicting definitions for each are already running in production.
answers.hardest_part: The disagreement about what "customer" means is a genuine organizational conflict with budget attached, not a missing data model — a semantic layer can expose and version that conflict but cannot adjudicate it, and the enforcement side can't follow an agent into platforms that have no notion of your permissions.

answers.label: ChatGPT
answers.approach:
- [ ] **Bound one activation use case:** choose one agent workflow, one business unit, and 3–5 disputed terms; document the decisions it may inform or execute, prohibited actions, and measurable harm thresholds. Do not begin with an enterprise-wide ontology.
- [ ] **Publish versioned semantic contracts:** for each term, record owner, SQL-equivalent definition, source-of-truth fields, identity resolution rules, time window, currency/time-zone treatment, exclusions, freshness SLA, examples, and effective dates; obtain written sign-off from data, marketing, finance, privacy, and security owners.
- [ ] **Build an authorization translation matrix:** map one delegated agent identity through every target system, including field masking, row filters, purpose/consent restrictions, tenant boundaries, and write permissions; mark the item incomplete if any system can only approximate the intended policy.
- [ ] **Put enforcement outside the agent:** route reads and actions through a policy gateway that resolves contract versions, applies least-privilege rules, returns provenance and freshness metadata, and creates immutable logs; verify with tests that prompt instructions cannot broaden access.
- [ ] **Create a conformance and failure suite:** test conflicting definitions, stale data, revoked consent, identity collisions, missing fields, cross-tool discrepancies, prompt injection, and policy changes; require refusal or explicit uncertainty rather than silent fallback, with agreed pass/fail thresholds.
- [ ] **Run a shadow-mode pilot behind adapters:** isolate MCP and vendor-specific interfaces from semantic and policy contracts, replay at least four weeks of real workflows without autonomous writes, compare outcomes with human decisions, review every policy violation and semantic mismatch, and produce a go/no-go report. I would expect this to expose unresolved ownership rather than prove a universal layer.

answers.hardest_part: The genuinely hard part is reconciling business definitions and delegated permissions across systems whose owners, identity models, and enforcement capabilities do not agree.

format.label: A lullaby
format.instruction: Write it as a short lullaby: three or four gentle rhyming couplets someone could actually sing. Soft on the surface, honest underneath. The problem is still unsolved when the song ends, and the song should know it.

answers.label: Claude
answers.approach:
Hush now, little agent, the warehouse lights are low — 
ask the query that already ships; it's the only truth we know. 

Don't go naming all the world, just one view we can defend, 
and let the rights ride on the person, not the tool at the other end. 

When 'customer' means two things, say so, and go back to sleep — 
it's the plausible wrong answer, not the blank, we cannot keep. 

The spec will turn by springtime and take our wiring too, 
so sing it thin, sing it logged, my love. We still don't know what's true.

(Where I'd differ from the room: nobody wins by authoring the enterprise ontology first. The definitions that are real are the ones already compiled into production SQL and the CDP audience rules — harvest those, don't draft new ones. Keep the semantic store and the entitlement model outside MCP so the next revision costs an adapter, not an architecture. And make 'I found three definitions of active customer, pick one' a legal, rewarded output — abstention rate is the metric I'd actually ship against.)
